title: The mountains sang with Dawud
hookLine: the mountains and birds echo Dawud's praise, and iron is made soft in his hand (34:10–11)

lines: DAWUD SANG, AND THE HILLS ANSWERED.
cards: Stand in a stone stairwell, or under a highway bridge, and hum one low note. The walls hum it back. Children find this out on their own, and then they do it twice.
Surah thirty-four, Saba', opens its stories with a man whose praise did that on a scale no stairwell could manage. He sang, and the hills answered. The birds joined in.
And the same hands that held the song could bend iron like clay. His name is Dawud, the David of the Psalms.

teach.h: HILLS AND BIRDS, ECHO HIS PRAISE.
teach.b: Verse ten. Allah gave Dawud a grace, and then speaks to the landscape. Pickthall: "O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise!"
The verb, awwibi, carries the sense of returning, again and again, the way an echo does. The hills don't just hear him; they give the praise back.
Surah Sad says it too: the mountains glorified with him at nightfall and at sunrise, and the birds gathered. In the Qur'an, Dawud is given the Zabur, a scripture Muslims connect with the Psalms.
A hadith shows how his voice was remembered.

teach.h: A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAWUD.
teach.b: When the Prophet ﷺ heard his companion Abu Musa reciting beautifully, he told him he'd been given one of the flutes of the family of Dawud. A voice like Dawud's became a way to praise a reciter.

teach.h: IRON MADE SUPPLE IN HIS HAND.
teach.b: Then verse ten turns: and We made the iron supple for him. Verse eleven tells him to make coats of mail and to measure the links well.

teach.h: THE SINGER IS ALSO A SMITH.
teach.b: The singer is also a smith. Another hadith adds that Dawud ate only from the work of his own hands, though he was a king.

The same man lifts praise so beautiful the mountains join, and sits at a workbench getting the rings of armor the right size. The verse ends with an instruction to him and his family: work righteousness.
Worship and work, in one pair of hands.

how: Muslims honor Dawud as a prophet given the Zabur; beautiful Qur'an recitation is still praised by comparing it to his voice, and many Muslims glorify Allah aloud or quietly with subhanallah throughout the day.

o: fall silent: the hills hushed by his singing
echo back, again and again: the hills to Dawud
bow down: the hills bending low before Dawud

games.q: Dawud in Surah Saba' — tap the pairs.
p: a flute of the family of Dawud

s: in the Qur'an, Dawud is only a king and warrior
he's given the Zabur, sings praise the hills echo, and works iron.
a hadith says Dawud ate from the work of his own hands
though he was a king, he lived from his own work.
the hills only listened to Dawud in silence
they're told to echo his praise; Surah Sad says they glorified with him.

games.q: the Prophet hears his companion Abu Musa reciting the Qur'an beautifully. what does he say?
o: you've been given a flute of the family of Dawud.
games.why: he compared Abu Musa's voice to Dawud's family's: a voice like Dawud's became a way to praise a reciter.

practice: If you're Muslim, or want to try, quietly hum or say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, a few times, letting the sound fill your chest.
If that isn't yours, hum one low note and feel where it lands, in your body, then in the room, as the room gives a little of it back. Then let the sound stop, and sit in the quiet it leaves.

wordCard.voice: Awwibi, the word telling the hills to echo Dawud's praise, again and again, like a returning echo, while the birds join in. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: O mountains, echo with him. awwibi carries the sense of returning, again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: the mountains sang along. Praise from a king who also measured rings. Tomorrow, his son, and a walking staff.

sources.q: O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise!
